content: Myocarditis is defined as inflammation of the myocardium, the muscular layer of the heart wall. It can manifest with symptoms such as chest pain, ST-segment elevation on an electrocardiogram, elevated biomarkers indicative of myocardial necrosis, heart failure, or even sudden cardiac death. Clinically, myocarditis can be categorized into fulminant myocarditis, acute myocarditis, chronic active myocarditis, and chronic persistent myocarditis. The inflammatory response in myocarditis may result in myocardial cell death (myonecrosis) either directly due to an infectious agent or indirectly as part of an autoimmune reaction triggered by infection or hypersensitivity. Life-threatening causes of myocarditis include carbon monoxide poisoning and Dengue fever. Common causes include infections (e.g., Lyme disease) and certain medications. Idiopathic myocarditis, the most prevalent form, is often suspected to be secondary to a viral infection. It is crucial to differentiate myocarditis from pericarditis and ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), as these conditions have distinct management strategies. In young adults, myocarditis accounts for up to 20% of sudden death cases. It is slightly more common in males than females. Most cases of myocarditis are self-limiting and associated with a favorable prognosis, particularly when secondary to a viral infection. However, in rare cases, complications such as cardiac failure, pulmonary edema, arrhythmias, or cardiogenic shock may occur. Fulminant myocarditis, if survived during the acute phase, has a better long-term prognosis compared to acute or giant cell myocarditis. Physical examination findings in myocarditis may include tachycardia, a cardiac gallop, mitral regurgitation due to left ventricular dilation, and pedal edema indicative of heart failure. A pericardial friction rub may be present if there is concurrent pericarditis, a condition sometimes referred to as myopericarditis. Historically, myocarditis was first described by Jean Baptiste Senac in 1794, and the term myocarditis was introduced by Joseph Friedrich Sobernheim in 1837. In the 1980s, the World Health Organization and the International Society and Federation of Cardiology distinguished myocarditis from other cardiomyopathies. The Dallas criteria, published in 1986, provided guidelines for the histopathological classification of myocarditis. Myocarditis can be classified based on causative, histological, and clinicopathological criteria. Causative classifications include infectious, immune-mediated, and toxic myocarditis. Histologically, it can be divided into lymphocytic, eosinophilic, polymorphic, giant cell myocarditis, and cardiac sarcoidosis. Clinicopathological subtypes include acute, fulminant, chronic active, and chronic persistent myocarditis. The pathophysiology of myocarditis involves an inflammatory response that may lead to myocyte destruction and left ventricular dysfunction. This process can occur during infections or hypersensitivity reactions, either directly or as part of an autoimmune mechanism. Life-threatening causes of myocarditis include carbon monoxide poisoning and Dengue fever. Common causes include infections such as Lyme disease and certain medications. Idiopathic myocarditis, the most common type, is often linked to viral infections. Myocarditis must be distinguished from pericarditis and STEMI, as these conditions require different treatments. There are no established risk factors for myocarditis, and routine screening is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. The global incidence of myocarditis is approximately 10 to 20 cases per 100,000 individuals, with younger individuals being more commonly affected. Males are slightly more frequently affected than females, and there is no racial predilection. In developed countries, viral infections, particularly Coxsackie B and enteroviruses, are the most common causes. In South America, Chagas disease caused by Trypanosoma cruzi is the leading cause. The natural history of myocarditis is usually self-limiting, with a good prognosis, especially when secondary to a viral infection. Rarely, patients may develop complications such as chronic dilated cardiomyopathy, heart block, congestive heart failure, pericarditis, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias, or sudden cardiac death. Fulminant myocarditis, if survived during the acute phase, has a better prognosis than acute or giant cell myocarditis. Certain clinical features, such as syncope, pulmonary hypertension, biventricular dysfunction, left bundle branch block, Q waves, AV block, and a left ventricular ejection fraction below 40%, are associated with sudden death and the need for cardiac transplantation. Diagnosis of myocarditis involves a combination of clinical history, physical examination, laboratory findings, imaging studies, and sometimes endomyocardial biopsy. A history of recent viral illness within the preceding 2-4 weeks is often elicited. Symptoms may include chest pain, pedal edema, palpitations, fever, and joint pain. Physical examination may reveal tachycardia, a cardiac gallop, mitral regurgitation, and pedal edema. Laboratory findings may show elevated markers of myocardial necrosis (e.g., CK-MB, cardiac troponins), inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP, ESR), and leukocytosis. Serologic markers such as Fas, Fas ligand, interleukin-10, and antimyosin autoantibodies may have prognostic value. Electrocardiogram (ECG) findings in myocarditis can mimic pericarditis or myocardial infarction, with ST-segment elevation being a common feature. Arrhythmias and heart block may also be observed. Endomyocardial biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosing and subclassifying myocarditis. Histopathological features include myocardial edema, inflammatory infiltrates rich in lymphocytes and macrophages, and focal myocyte destruction. Imaging studies such as chest X-ray, echocardiography, cardiac CT, and cardiac MRI are valuable in the diagnosis and management of myocarditis. Echocardiography can assess left ventricular dysfunction and distinguish fulminant from acute myocarditis. Cardiac MRI can detect myocardial inflammation, edema, and fibrosis, with characteristic patterns of gadolinium enhancement. Treatment of myocarditis is primarily supportive, with symptomatic management being the cornerstone of therapy. Diuretics and inotropes may be used for left ventricular failure, and ACE inhibitors can aid in left ventricular remodeling. In fulminant myocarditis, mechanical circulatory support such as intra-aortic balloon pumps or left ventricular assist devices may be necessary. Antimicrobial therapy is recommended for bacterial myocarditis, and immunosuppressive therapy may be effective in giant cell myocarditis, autoimmune myocarditis, and eosinophilic myocarditis. Arrhythmias should be treated only if symptomatic or sustained, and temporary pacemakers may be required for conduction abnormalities. Cardiac transplantation may be necessary for refractory cases, particularly in giant cell myocarditis, although recurrence of the condition can occur post-transplant. There are no established measures for the primary prevention of myocarditis, but vaccination against diseases such as measles, rubella, mumps, poliomyelitis, and influenza can prevent myocarditis secondary to these infections. Secondary prevention includes clinical evaluation, ECG, echocardiography, and advanced imaging modalities such as cardiac MRI or CT when indicated. Regular cardiac function assessments are recommended at one and six months post-diagnosis and annually thereafter.
